entries.note: Means a living, breathing thing; one definition of the Latin root specifies a nonhuman creature, though 14th-century English usage could include humans.
Animals with mammary glands that suckle their young; related to [[mama]] and, Rob notes, to the place name [[Manchester]].
Rob says the place name is related to the mammary gland and [[mama]], referring to breast-shaped hills.
Means flat-footed and shares the foot ending of [[octopus]], so platypuses, platypi and platypodes all have etymological precedent as plurals.
Built from Greek elements for eight and foot but never a Greek word; Jess argues octopuses, octopi and octopodes are all justifiable, while Rob prefers octopuses.
The actual Greek word for the octopus, which passed into Latin as polypus and then into English; it inspired the medical term [[polyp]].
Medical term inspired by [[polypus]], as the growth looks like a sea creature attached to the body; its plural is also murky.
Cited as sharing the foot element of [[octopus]] yet pluralized the English way, as isopods.
From a Latin word meaning crawling, describing animals that are low to the ground.
Literally means double life, from amphi and bios as in biology; related to the Latin prefix [[ambi-]].
Theaters with seating on both sides; the amphi element can mean all around but also specifically both, as in [[amphibian]].
Able to use both hands, literally right-handed on both sides, from [[ambi-]]; Rob wonders whether anyone can really have two right hands.
Mentioned as the Latin for left-handed, the counterpart to the right-handedness in [[ambidextrous]].
Shares an ancient root with Latin piscis, as in [[Pisces]]; Old English fisc; similar words appear across Indo-European languages, though biologically there's arguably no such thing as a fish.
Entered English in the 1400s meaning scoundrel, villain or swindler, naming the fish only from the 1700s; origin uncertain, probably Germanic.
The Old Norse word for shark, related to Dutch [[haai]] and German [[Hai]]; Old English lacked a general word for sharks.
The French word for shark, whose meaning Jess finds scary; the explanation is garbled in the transcript.
The Greek word for shark, literally jagged biter.
An old seafaring term for a shark that Rob found; Jess links it to Melville calling brown sharks [[sea attorney|sea attorneys]].
Herman Melville's name for brown sharks in a book other than Moby-Dick; compared to [[water lawyer]].
Melville's name for the white shark, alongside [[sea attorney]] for brown sharks.
Animals without vertebrae, from vertebra meaning joint, referring to the joints of the spine; hence they're spineless.
From Latin for cut into, meaning segmented; the Romans translated the Greek word behind [[entomology]], like calling them cut-ups.
Its Greek root means cut into, like [[insect]] in Latin; confusing it with [[etymology]] inspires a joke Jess hears almost daily.
From the Greek word for spider; the group also includes scorpions, mites and ticks.
Praying as in to a god, not preying, a fitting eggcorn; mantis means diviner or seer, sharing a PIE root with [[mnemonic]] and [[memory]].
From Latin mollis, soft, originally the gooey ones before shelled species were included; related to French [[moelleux]] and English [[melt]].
A French word for something soft and oozing, like a chocolate cake; related to [[mollusk]].
Thought to be a sailors' variant of [[squirt]], referring to its inking; a group is a shoal, though some advocate calling it a squad.
From Latin calamarius, pertaining to pens, related to a word for reed; Jess corrects Rob that calligraphy is unrelated.
From Latin crusta, shell, referring to their hard exoskeletons; basically the opposite of [[mollusk]] in crunchiness.
Probably a euphemism meaning the brown thing, as people were too scared to say the original name, perhaps related to [[arktos]].
Rob half-remembers that the arktos-type words for bear may themselves be euphemisms related to honey, so the original name for [[bear]] is lost.
Rob's 'dog mystery': its origin is unknown, other languages only borrow it, and its -og ending recurs in [[frog]], [[hog]], [[stag]] and [[pig]].
A French word for certain dog breeds, borrowed from English [[dog]].
Other Germanic languages use a word like hound for dog; it shares a PIE root with [[canine]] and, via Greek, with [[cynic]].
Means doglike, from Greek; the Cynics were perhaps named for their wandering lifestyle or the [[Kynosarges]] gymnasium; shares a PIE root with [[hound]].
A gymnasium near Athens where Antisthenes taught, possibly the source of the name [[cynic]].
German and Dutch have words like Frosch and vors; Old English had frosc but switched to a form like frogga, perhaps to be cute, like [[dog]].
Another unexplained -og word like [[dog]]; similar Celtic words exist, but Old English hog meant males of almost any farm animal, complicating that origin.
Another odd -g word like [[dog]]; originally a male deer in its fifth year, with related words elsewhere meaning males of various species.
Has no obvious Germanic precedent; its earliest trace is [[picbred]], an acorn, perhaps pig bread; like [[dog]], an unsatisfying mystery.
An Old English term for an acorn, probably meaning pig feed, and the earliest trace of [[pig]].
Of unknown origin, originally brid before its letters swapped; no corresponding word exists in other Germanic or Romance languages.
Means [[pig]] fish, as discussed in an earlier episode.
From an Afrikaans word meaning earth [[pig]].
From Old French for spiny or thorny [[pig]]; it has had many spellings, including pork despine, porkpen and Shakespeare's porpentine in Hamlet.
Once much closer to [[Alcatraz]] but probably influenced by Latin albus, white, for the big white birds.
Portuguese for pelican, from an Arabic word meaning sea eagle; the rock presumably had many pelicans; the source of [[albatross]].
From an Old French phrase meaning foot of a crane, as forked genealogical charts resembled a crane's long toes.
From Spanish el lagarto, the lizard; English briefly said lagarto before adding the al-, which, unlike most al- words, isn't Arabic.
Exact origin unknown; Greek krokodilos, pebble worm, was probably ancient folk etymology; English once preferred cocodrille, from French and medieval Latin, perhaps via bestiaries.
Means river horse; the potamus part meaning river also appears in [[Mesopotamia]].
Means between rivers, sharing its river element with [[hippopotamus]].
Another name for the seahorse, literally horse sea monster; also the seahorse-shaped part of the brain.
Shares a PIE root meaning water creature with [[hydra]]; in 17th-century English, sea otters were sometimes called sea apes.
From Malay; the hosts can't settle whether it means person of the forest or old man of the forest and leave it as homework.
Means ghost in Latin, perhaps because of their little white faces and nocturnal movements.
From Malay, literally something that rolls up.
The hosts struggle with elk versus [[moose]]: they are different animals, but moose are called elk in some parts of the world.
Bigger than the [[elk]] and a different animal, though moose are called elk in some parts of the world.
The same species as [[reindeer]]; caribou is used for those in North America, reindeer for those in Europe and elsewhere.
American bison are sometimes called buffalo but technically aren't; true buffalo live elsewhere and look like humped cows; buffalo is also a verb meaning to bully.

entries.term: Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo
entries.note: A grammatical sentence using [[buffalo]] as the animal, the city and a verb meaning to bully; a particularly egregious [[garden path sentence]].
A sentence you must reread once you reach the end, because it led you up the garden path, as in 'the horse raced past the barn fell'.
Has basically always meant cat, with nearly identical words across Europe; many languages also have a cute hissing, plosive-sibilant word or call for cats.
Hides a cat: means ground lion or dwarf lion, its first part going back to a root meaning low down.
The French word for bat, literally bald mouse, which Jess finds an odd feature to name it for rather than flying.
Jess says the name refers to the way it bats its wings.
Latin musculus meant both muscle and little mouse, supposedly because flexing muscles looked like mice running under the skin; compare [[lacertous]].
A short-lived English word meaning muscular, literally lizardy, for the same reason as [[muscle]].
The German word for placenta; Rob notes German medical terms are often literal, whereas English euphemizes through Greek and Latin.
From Latin peculium, property in cattle; hence belonging solely to, then distinguished or special for someone rich in cows, then odd.
Relates to cows: Edward Jenner prevented smallpox by injecting a small amount of cowpox, so to vaccinate is literally to 'cow-ize'.
Means pleasantly pastoral, literally cow-tending, from Greek elements for cow and tending.
Named as a supposed hybrid of lion and [[panther]]; English kept French leupart's pronunciation after the French re-added the Latin o to the spelling.
Thought to mean something like all beasts, though that may be folk etymology applied to a word from another language.
From Guarani and Tupi, where the full word means true carnivore: the final part means true, and the rest is their general word for carnivore.
From French for lion's tooth, after the jagged leaves; also called blowballs, clocks, [[piss-a-bed]], [[cankerwort]], milk witch and Irish daisy.
An old name for the [[dandelion]], alongside peabed and wet-a-bed, probably because it was used as a diuretic.
An old name for the [[dandelion]] meaning something like crab grass, tied to crabs and [[cancer]], discussed in an earlier episode.
Badger hound, from the Old High German for badger; bred to chase badgers into their holes, hence the sausage shape.
The Welsh word for dwarf dog.
Usually translated as little brushwood dog, referring to either their fur color or the landscape they were bred to hunt in.
Said to be an ancient Sumerian word meaning plunge earth, as Bedouin hunters launched the dogs off camels' backs for a running start.
From Chinese, literally lion dog, another word hiding a lion.
German for growler.
From Lingala, spoken in the northeastern Congo; its full name is a phrase thought to mean dog of the villagers, a local tamed dog.
Originally an insult for humans meaning mutton-head, then for dogs (perhaps dim or scolded for sheep worrying), and now insults humans again.
